segments.title: Induced demand omitted from business cases
segments.quote: Traffic engineers have known this since the sixties and it has a name, induced demand, and it gets left out of every business case I have ever read including this one.
segments.full_text: It makes driving slightly better, which over ten years makes driving slightly more attractive, which puts more cars on the road, which uses up the capacity the system created. Traffic engineers have known this since the sixties and it has a name, induced demand, and it gets left out of every business case I have ever read including this one.

codes.rationale: Long-term traffic consequences and induced demand are systematically omitted from business cases.

segments.title: Passing the long-term question to someone else
segments.quote: Every actor here has a defensible reason why the long-term question belongs to someone else, and the sum of those defensible reasons is that it belongs to nobody.
segments.full_text: [Interviewer] Was that raised during planning? [Respondent] I raised it at a workshop. The response was that the system is signal timing, not transport policy, and induced demand is a policy question. Which is true and also a way of ensuring nobody owns it. Every actor here has a defensible reason why the long-term question belongs to someone else, and the sum of those defensible reasons is that it belongs to nobody.

codes.rationale: Institutional compartmentalization is used defensively to avoid ownership of systemic long-term consequences.

segments.title: Scenario workshop with diverse stakeholders
segments.quote: We did, with about thirty people — planners, two councillors, a bus operator, four residents, a freight association. Three scenarios out to 2040.
segments.full_text: [Interviewer] You ran a scenario workshop yourself, I think? [Respondent] We did, with about thirty people — planners, two councillors, a bus operator, four residents, a freight association. Three scenarios out to 2040. The useful part wasn't the scenarios, it was that the freight association and the disability group ended up agreeing about kerb space, which neither of them expected and neither would have discovered in a consultation questionnaire.

codes.rationale: Exploring multiple alternative scenarios out to 2040 with a diverse group.
Upstream, two-way participatory workshop enabling unexpected alignment between non-expert and institutional actors.

segments.title: Submitting workshop outputs to the local plan
segments.quote: Into the local plan consultation, where it sits alongside four hundred other submissions. I'd call that neither success nor failure.
segments.full_text: [Interviewer] Did the workshop output go anywhere? [Respondent] Into the local plan consultation, where it sits alongside four hundred other submissions. I'd call that neither success nor failure. It's in the record. Sometimes things in the record get picked up years later by someone you've never met. I've stopped measuring impact on a three-year cycle because nothing in planning works on a three-year cycle.

codes.rationale: Outputs are absorbed into a consultation record without generating adaptive changes or institutional responsiveness.

segments.title: Undisclosed objective function of the system
segments.quote: Publish the objective function. One page, plain language: here is what the system is trying to maximise, here is what it treats as a cost, here is who decided.
segments.full_text: [Interviewer] If the city asked you what to change tomorrow, what would you say? [Respondent] Publish the objective function. One page, plain language: here is what the system is trying to maximise, here is what it treats as a cost, here is who decided. Nobody can argue with a system whose goals are undisclosed, and at the moment nobody outside the vendor knows what it is optimising.

codes.rationale: Critical highlighting of opaque, unexamined technical assumptions and hidden optimization criteria embedded by the vendor.

summary: The respondent, an associate professor of urban planning, provides a critical account of the Port Calder traffic system that highlights significant gaps in anticipation, reflexivity, engagement, and responsiveness. Anticipation is undermined by deterministic short-term business cases that deliberately exclude long-term phenomena like induced demand. Reflexivity is challenged by institutional fragmentation, where actors disclaim responsibility for systemic consequences, and by opaque vendor-controlled objective functions. Public engagement is demonstrated positively through an upstream scenario workshop that fostered unexpected alignment between diverse stakeholders, contrasting with passive downstream consultation processes. Finally, responsiveness is shown to be weak, as substantive inputs are relegated to consultation archives rather than driving adaptive policy shifts. The multi-coded segment on the scenario workshop illustrates how participatory foresight can bridge anticipation and inclusive engagement.
transcript:
Interview transcript A04 — Associate professor of urban planning
Case: Port Calder adaptive traffic signal and pedestrian detection system  |  SYNTHETIC DATA — not a real interview
[Interviewer] What's your reading of what this system does to the city?
[Respondent] It makes driving slightly better, which over ten years makes driving slightly more attractive, which puts more cars on the road, which uses up the capacity the system created. Traffic engineers have known this since the sixties and it has a name, induced demand, and it gets left out of every business case I have ever read including this one.
[Interviewer] Was that raised during planning?
[Respondent] I raised it at a workshop. The response was that the system is signal timing, not transport policy, and induced demand is a policy question. Which is true and also a way of ensuring nobody owns it. Every actor here has a defensible reason why the long-term question belongs to someone else, and the sum of those defensible reasons is that it belongs to nobody.
[Interviewer] You ran a scenario workshop yourself, I think?
[Respondent] We did, with about thirty people — planners, two councillors, a bus operator, four residents, a freight association. Three scenarios out to 2040. The useful part wasn't the scenarios, it was that the freight association and the disability group ended up agreeing about kerb space, which neither of them expected and neither would have discovered in a consultation questionnaire.
[Interviewer] Did the workshop output go anywhere?
[Respondent] Into the local plan consultation, where it sits alongside four hundred other submissions. I'd call that neither success nor failure. It's in the record. Sometimes things in the record get picked up years later by someone you've never met. I've stopped measuring impact on a three-year cycle because nothing in planning works on a three-year cycle.
[Interviewer] If the city asked you what to change tomorrow, what would you say?
[Respondent] Publish the objective function. One page, plain language: here is what the system is trying to maximise, here is what it treats as a cost, here is who decided. Nobody can argue with a system whose goals are undisclosed, and at the moment nobody outside the vendor knows what it is optimising.
